facts.text: Tristan und Isolde premiered in Munich on 10 June 1865, conducted by Hans von Bülow.
facts.evidence: premiered at the Königliches Hoftheater und Nationaltheater in Munich on 10 June 1865, with Hans von Bülow conducting

facts.text: The premiere, planned for 15 May 1865, was postponed because the Isolde, Malvina Schnorr von Carolsfeld, was hoarse. Her husband Ludwig sang Tristan.
evidence: The planned premiere on 15 May 1865 had to be postponed until the Isolde, Malvina Schnorr von Carolsfeld, had recovered from hoarseness
with Malvina's husband Ludwig partnering her as Tristan

facts.text: The opera was inspired partly by Schopenhauer’s philosophy and by Wagner’s relationship with his muse, Mathilde Wesendonck.
facts.evidence: Tristan und Isolde was inspired in part by the philosophy of Arthur Schopenhauer, and by Wagner's relationship with his muse Mathilde Wesendonck.

facts.text: Wagner to Liszt, 1854: “Never in my life having enjoyed the true happiness of love I shall erect a memorial to this loveliest of all dreams.”
facts.attribution: Wagner, letter to Franz Liszt (via Wikipedia)
facts.evidence: Never in my life having enjoyed the true happiness of love I shall erect a memorial to this loveliest of all dreams

facts.text: The “Tristan chord” in the Prelude marks a defining moment in music history: chromaticism, tonal ambiguity and prolonged harmonic suspension.
evidence: Its advanced harmony, immediately announced by the Tristan chord of its prelude, marks a defining moment in the evolution of music

facts.text: The harmonic tension set up in the Prelude isn’t fully resolved until the very end of Act III.
facts.evidence: The cadences first introduced in the prelude are not resolved until the finale of act 3

facts.text: Critic Eduard Hanslick, 1868: the Prelude reminded him of an old painting of a martyr whose intestines are slowly unwound on a reel.
facts.evidence: reminds one of the old Italian painting of a martyr [Erasmus of Formia] whose intestines are slowly unwound from his body on a reel

facts.text: Emmanuel Chabrier reportedly wept at the opening: “I’ve been waiting for ten years of my life for that A on the ’cellos.”
facts.evidence: I've been waiting for ten years of my life for that A on the 'cellos

facts.text: Clara Schumann called Tristan “the most repugnant thing I have ever seen or heard in all my life”.
facts.evidence: the most repugnant thing I have ever seen or heard in all my life

facts.text: Verdi said, shortly before his death, that he “stood in wonder and terror” before Tristan.
Richard Strauss first said Wagner’s music “would kill a cat”. Later, after conducting his first Tristan: “It was the most wonderful day of my life.”
evidence: would kill a cat and would turn rocks into scrambled eggs
I have conducted my first Tristan.
It was the most wonderful day of my life.

facts.text: Mark Twain at Bayreuth: “I know of some, and have heard of many, who could not sleep after it, but cried the night away.”
facts.evidence: I know of some, and have heard of many, who could not sleep after it, but cried the night away.

facts.text: At the climax of the love duet, the expected resolution is cut off by Kurwenal’s cry: “Rette Dich, Tristan!”
facts.evidence: where Tristan and Isolde gradually build up to a musical climax only to have the expected resolution interrupted by Kurwenal ("Rette Dich, Tristan!")

facts.text: Ravel parodied this love duet as a duet for two cats in L’enfant et les sortilèges.
facts.evidence: Maurice Ravel parodied the Love Duet in the Duo miaulé in his opera L'enfant et les sortilèges

facts.text: Only after Isolde’s “Liebestod” does the music fully resolve; she sinks down, “as if transfigured”, onto Tristan’s body.
facts.evidence: Full resolution does not occur until the very end, after Isolde sings the passage commonly called the "Liebestod"

facts.text: Wagner himself called the Prelude the “Liebestod” and Isolde’s final aria the “Verklärung” (Transfiguration).
facts.evidence: Wagner called the prelude the "Liebestod" (Love-death) while Isolde's final aria "Mild und leise" he called the "Verklärung" (Transfiguration).

facts.text: The first Tristan, Ludwig Schnorr von Carolsfeld, died suddenly in July 1865 after singing the role only four times.
evidence: On 21 July 1865, having sung the role only four times, Ludwig died suddenly

facts.text: Two conductors, Felix Mottl (1911) and Joseph Keilberth (1968), died after collapsing while conducting Act II of Tristan.
evidence: The stress of performing Tristan also claimed the lives of conductors Felix Mottl in 1911 and Joseph Keilberth in 1968. Both died after collapsing while conducting the second act.

facts.text: The Met gave the first American performance on 1 December 1886, with Lilli Lehmann and Albert Niemann.
facts.evidence: The first American performance was held at the Metropolitan Opera on 1 December 1886, with Albert Niemann and Lilli Lehmann
